signals.observation: Forms of ἀθάνατος recur eight times, moving from Socrates' question about an immortal thing, to the assertion that the soul is immortal, to the requirement that an interlocutor acknowledge immortal souls, to arguments about the nature of immortals, and finally to the soul's kinship with the immortal.

signals.observation: Forms of κακός recur throughout the section as the central term in the argument, beginning with the general question of good and evil, moving through the specific evil that makes each thing bad, and culminating in the soul's condition affected by countless evils.

signals.observation: Forms of πονηρία recur eight times in a dense concentration, moving from the general statement that each thing's wickedness destroys it, through the extended argument about food's wickedness and the body, to the conclusion that the soul's own wickedness cannot destroy it.

signals.observation: The contrast between οἰκεῖος (one's own) and ἀλλότριος (another's) recurs as the central distinction in the argument about what can destroy the soul, with the claim that only its own evil could destroy it, not another's.

elements.context: ἀδικία τε καὶ ἀκολασία καὶ δειλία καὶ ἀμαθία

ἐναργέστερον δικαιοσύνας τε καὶ ἀδικίας διόψεται

signals.observation: Forms of ἀδικία recur six times, beginning as one of the evils that makes the soul bad, examined as potentially destroying the soul, tested as possibly being deadly like a disease, declared not terrible if it were deadly, and finally mentioned as something that will be seen more clearly when the soul is viewed in its pure state.

elements.context: τὴν ἀδικίαν εἶναι θανάσιμον τῷ ἔχοντι ὥσπερ νόσον

signals.observation: Forms of θανάσιμος appear three times in a brief sequence, testing whether injustice is deadly to the one who possesses it and concluding that injustice is very far from being deadly.

elements.context: τοὺς μὲν μάλιστα θᾶττον, τοὺς δʼ ἧττον σχολαίτερον... ἀποθνῄσκειν

signals.observation: Forms of ἀποθνῄσκω recur four times in close sequence, examining whether the souls of those dying become more unjust through death, whether the one dying becomes worse, and whether the unjust die by injustice itself or by others imposing penalty.

elements.context: ἕως ἂν εἰς θάνατον ἀγαγοῦσα τοῦ σώματος χωρίσῃ
τῶν ἀποθνῃσκόντων ἀδικώτεραι αἱ ψυχαὶ διὰ τὸν θάνατον γίγνονται

signals.observation: θάνατον appears twice, first as the potential end point if injustice were to lead the soul to death and separate it from the body, and then in the question of whether souls become more unjust through death.

elements.context: τὸ μὲν ἀπολλύον καὶ διαφθεῖρον πᾶν τὸ κακὸν εἶναι

signals.observation: Forms of διαφθείρω recur four times, establishing the general principle that evil corrupts and destroys, examining whether anything else can corrupt what its own evil cannot, and concluding that the soul cannot be corrupted by another's evil without its own.

signals.observation: Forms of νόσος and νόσημα recur five times, establishing disease as the innate evil of the body, comparing wickedness to disease, and testing whether injustice might be deadly like a disease.

signals.observation: Forms of σῶμα recur fourteen times, beginning with the body's disease, developing the analogy between the body's destruction by its own evil and the soul's potential destruction, and concluding with the soul's association with the body that has obscured its true nature.

elements.context: κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τοίνυν λόγον... ἔχει γάρ, ἔφη, λόγον

signals.observation: The phrase ἔχει γάρ, ἔφη, λόγον appears as Glaucon's acknowledgment that Socrates' argument according to the same reasoning makes sense.

elements.context: οὐ λελωβημένον δεῖ αὐτὸ θεάσασθαι

signals.observation: Forms of θεάομαι recur four times in a close sequence, contrasting the need to view the soul unmutilated with the present viewing of it in its current condition, and comparing this present viewing to viewing the sea-god Glaucus.

elements.context: ἐννόει γάρ, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, ὦ Γλαύκων

signals.observation: Glaucon is addressed by name at 609e and 611d, and between these direct addresses the sea-god Glaucus (θαλάττιον Γλαῦκον) is mentioned as a figure whose ancient nature cannot easily be seen because of accretions.

elements.context: τὰ μὲν ἐκκεκλάσθαι
τὰ δὲ συντετρῖφθαι
πάντως λελωβῆσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν κυμάτων

οὐ λελωβημένον δεῖ αὐτὸ θεάσασθαι

signals.observation: A cluster of perfect passive participles describes the condition of the sea-god Glaucus: parts broken off, worn down, mutilated by waves, and other things grown upon him; this is preceded by the statement that the soul must be viewed not mutilated (λελωβημένον).

elements.context: ὄστρεά τε καὶ φυκία καὶ πέτρας
περικρουσθεῖσα πέτρας τε καὶ ὄστρεα

signals.observation: ὄστρεα appears twice, first describing the shells grown upon the sea-god Glaucus, then describing what the soul would be knocked free from if it followed its impulse toward the divine.

elements.context: ὄστρεά τε καὶ φυκία καὶ πέτρας
περικρουσθεῖσα πέτρας τε καὶ ὄστρεα
γεηρὰ καὶ πετρώδη πολλὰ καὶ ἄγρια

signals.observation: Forms related to πέτρα recur three times, first as rocks grown upon Glaucus, then as what the soul would be knocked free from, and finally as rocky things grown upon the soul because of earthly feastings.

elements.context: εἰς τὴν φιλοσοφίαν αὐτῆς

signals.observation: φιλοσοφίαν appears as that toward which one must look to understand what the soul touches and what companionships it desires.

elements.context: συγγενὴς οὖσα τῷ τε θείῳ καὶ ἀθανάτῳ
καὶ τῷ ἀεὶ ὄντι

signals.observation: The soul is described as kindred to the divine, the immortal, and that which always is, a triad of affiliations indicating its true nature.

elements.context: ἀνάγκη αὐτὸ ἀεὶ ὂν εἶναι· εἰ δʼ ἀεὶ ὄν, ἀθάνατον
ἐννοεῖς ὅτι ἀεὶ ἂν εἶεν αἱ αὐταί
καὶ τῷ ἀεὶ ὄντι

signals.observation: ἀεί recurs three times, establishing that the soul must always exist, that the same souls would always exist, and that the soul is kindred to that which always is.

elements.context: οὔτε γὰρ ἄν που ἐλάττους γένοιντο
οὔτε αὖ πλείους
εἰ γὰρ ὁτιοῦν τῶν ἀθανάτων πλέον γίγνοιτο

signals.observation: Comparative forms ἐλάττους and πλείους/πλέον appear in close proximity as part of the argument that immortal souls can become neither fewer nor more in number.

elements.context: ἐκ τοῦ θνητοῦ ἂν γίγνοιτο

signals.observation: θνητοῦ appears once in the argument that if immortals could increase in number, they would have to come from the mortal, and all things would end up being immortal.

elements.context: οὐ ῥᾴδιον, ἦν δʼ ἐγώ, ἀίδιον εἶναι σύνθετόν τε ἐκ πολλῶν
μὴ τῇ καλλίστῃ κεχρημένον συνθέσει

signals.observation: σύνθετον and συνθέσει appear together in the statement that it is not easy for something composite from many parts to be eternal unless it possesses the finest composition, which the soul has not been shown to have.

elements.context: πολλῆς ποικιλίας καὶ ἀνομοιότητός τε καὶ διαφορᾶς γέμειν

signals.observation: ποικιλίας appears in the warning not to think the soul in its truest nature is full of much variety, dissimilarity, and difference within itself.

elements.context: οἷόν ἐστιν καθαρὸν γιγνόμενον

signals.observation: καθαρὸν appears in the description of how the soul must be contemplated as it becomes pure, in contrast to its present mutilated condition.

elements.context: τοιοῦτον ἱκανῶς λογισμῷ διαθεατέον

signals.observation: λογισμῷ appears as the means by which the soul in its pure state must be contemplated thoroughly.

elements.context: ἐννοεῖν ὧν ἅπτεται καὶ οἵων ἐφίεται ὁμιλιῶν
ὧν ἅπτεται καὶ οἵων ἐφίεται ὁμιλιῶν

signals.observation: ἅπτεται and ἐφίεται appear together describing what the soul touches and what companionships it desires when one looks toward its philosophy.

elements.context: ὑπὸ ταύτης τῆς ὁρμῆς ἐκκομισθεῖσα ἐκ τοῦ πόντου ἐν ᾧ νῦν ἐστίν

signals.observation: The soul is described as being carried out from the sea in which it now is by the impulse toward the divine and eternal.

elements.context: ἅτε γῆν ἑστιωμένῃ
ὑπὸ τῶν εὐδαιμόνων λεγομένων ἑστιάσεων

signals.observation: Forms of ἑστιάω recur twice, describing the soul as feasting on earth and the earthy, rocky, wild things that have grown upon it from so-called blessed feastings.

elements.context: εἴτε πολυειδὴς εἴτε μονοειδής
εἴτε πολυειδὴς εἴτε μονοειδής

signals.observation: πολυειδὴς and μονοειδής are placed in direct contrast as alternative possibilities for the soul's true nature—whether it is many-formed or single-formed.

elements.context: τὰ ἐν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ βίῳ πάθη τε καὶ εἴδη
διὰ ταῦτα τὰ παθήματα τοῦ σώματος

signals.observation: πάθη appears describing the affections and forms in human life that have been discussed, earlier paired with παθήματα describing the sufferings of the body.

elements.context: τά γε μέγιστα ἐπίχειρα ἀρετῆς καὶ προκείμενα ἆθλα οὐ διεληλύθαμεν
δικαιοσύνας τε καὶ ἀδικίας διόψεται καὶ πάντα ἃ νῦν διήλθομεν
τὰ ἐν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ βίῳ πάθη τε καὶ εἴδη, ὡς ἐγᾦμαι, ἐπιεικῶς αὐτῆς διεληλύθαμεν

signals.observation: Forms of διέρχομαι recur three times, framing the section: opening with the statement that they have not gone through the greatest prizes, continuing with what has been gone through that will be seen more clearly, and closing with the fair account they have gone through of the affections and forms in human life.
